How can stronger institutions and better governance help countries create jobs, build climate resilience, and reduce emissions? Governance for Climate-Smart Development, a World Bank Group event at COP31, examines how policy reform and effective implementation can turn climate and development priorities into results. Drawing on evidence from over 100 economies covered by the World Bank Group’s Country Climate and Development Reports (CCDRs), country representatives will discuss:
• How institutions and governance support climate action
• How policy reforms can advance climate-smart development

items.description: Europe has weathered a series of shocks, but global risks continue to weigh heavily on the outlook. Sovereign yields have increased, defense and other spending pressures are rising, and persistently low productivity growth leaves the region with few if any buffers. This event will present and discuss the IMF report’s forecasts for the region and how Europe can choose growth through reforms for innovation, scale, and resilience. items.description: Stablecoins are changing how we think about digital payments. But how do they fit into the economy? In this episode of The Economy: How Do You Measure That?, Jim Tebrake and Artak Harutyunyan break down stablecoins, exploring how they are issued, used for payments, and measured in economic statistics.

items.title: Rights & Wrongs: Recap - Can the ICC Survive?
items.description:
The International Criminal Court (ICC) was created to try the worst crimes in the world – war crimes, genocide, crimes against humanity. Established in 1998 following the deadly civil war in Yugoslavia and genocide Rwanda, the ICC has indicted 63 suspects. Each of court’s 125 member states is obligated to arrest these suspects should they set foot in their territory, but the indictments of Russian President Vladimir Putin and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu are testing the member states’ resolve. And now the US is threatening to sanction the court. Can the ICC survive 2025?

items.title: How neutrality enables us to carry out our humanitarian work | ICRC
items.description:
Staying neutral allows us to do our job. It is not indifference: it is a deliberate choice.
 
Our mission comes from the Geneva Conventions, universal laws that preserve a degree of humanity, even in war. Today, 163 years since our founding, neutrality remains as crucial as ever.

items.title: Is Bitcoin really money?
items.description: Is Bitcoin really money? You can use it to buy a coffee, but in macroeconomic statistics, Bitcoin isn’t classified the way you might expect. In this episode of The Economy – How Do You Measure That, Jim Tebrake sits down with Padma Hurree Gobin to explain how statisticians classify Bitcoin, why they consider it an asset rather than money, and why the answer ultimately comes down to one simple question: Who owes whom?

items.title: Autonomous weapons: Who is responsible when AI decides to kill?
items.description:
Under international humanitarian law (IHL), military commanders remain accountable for ensuring that the conduct of hostilities complies with the laws of war and for protecting civilians from the effects of armed conflict.

As autonomous weapon systems advance, delegating life-and-death decisions to machines raises serious concerns about human control, accountability and compliance with IHL.

Discover why the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) is calling for legally binding rules to prohibit unpredictable autonomous weapons and ensure meaningful human control over the use of force

items.title: Humanitarian pauses, corridors and ceasefires: what do they mean for civilians? | ICRC
items.description:
Humanitarian pauses, corridors, ceasefires… are they defined by international humanitarian law? 

Whatever the term used, warring parties have obligations to protect civilians and aid workers.

Cordula Droege, ICRC's director of International Law, Movement and Partnerships, explains more.

items.title: Is That Government Fee Actually a Tax?
items.description:
Is that government fee actually a tax? A driver’s license, permit, or government fee isn’t always classified the way you might expect.

In this episode of The Economy – How Do You Measure That, Jim Tebrake sits down with Justine Ayebare to explain how statisticians distinguish between taxes and payments for government services, why the cost of providing the service matters, and why consistent classification is important for understanding government finances.

items.title: This is how we are supporting communities in Tigray, Ethiopia
items.description:
📍Ethiopia | In Tigray, we recently provided essential medical supplies to Chercher Primary Health Centre and the hospitals in Alamata, Mahoni and Lemlem Karl (Maychew), where recent hostilities have further strained access to healthcare.
 
With this support, we are trying to address shortages of medicines and medical supplies, enabling health facilities to continue providing care to people in need.
 
Healthcare facilities, medical personnel and patients must be protected during armed conflict. We continue to support access to healthcare for those affected.

items.title: How can ICRC's humanitarian action help lay the foundations for a more peaceful future?
items.description: This video explores how ICRC’s principled humanitarian action creates conditions conducive to peace and supports efforts to prevent and resolve armed conflict. Drawing on operational experiences in Colombia, Northern Ireland, and Yemen, the video highlights how protecting human dignity, strengthening local social cohesion, and acting as a neutral intermediary help build trust between parties and pave the way toward conflict resolution.

items.title: From Maryam in Nigeria to her husband, missing for ten years | ICRC
items.description:
📍Nigeria | Maryam lost four of her eight children to armed conflict and never got to see their bodies.

Ten years ago, her husband also went missing, leaving her to raise the children who remain while carrying the uncertainty of not knowing what happened to him.
 
Since then, joy has never felt the same. Still, she holds on to the hope that one day, he will come home.

items.title: Ben Bland on Southeast Asia in a Fragmented World
items.description:
Recent geopolitical shocks have changed the nature of international trade and left regional organizations to tighten their economic ties. The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), one of the world's most effective blocs, is now intensifying integration among its members to mitigate the effects of global fragmentation. Ben Bland is the director of the Asia-Pacific Programme at Chatham House. In this podcast, he says concentrations of economic power across the region are complicating matters.
